### Introduction

This project examines the differences in educational development and opportunity around the world. The quality of education among a country's population is a solid indicator of the wellbeing and future advancement of a country, yet it varies significantly across different places and groups of people. I was curious about the extent of these differences, so I turned to the data to find out.

I used data from the United Nations' Human Development Reports by the UN Development Program; I obtained data from [UNDP's open database](https://hdr.undp.org/data-center/documentation-and-downloads) which covers 34 years: 1990 to 2023. Note that the variables that I was interested in were missing data past 2023 so the last couple of years (2024 and 2025) aren't included in my analysis.

The data contains information on the educational attributes of countries' adults 25 and older.

I'll focus on the following main measures: the percentage of men and women (individually) with at least secondary education within a country, the average amount of formal education attained by men and women (individually) within a country, and the average amount of education attained by adults within a country. Secondary education, under the [UN's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED)](https://www.uis.unesco.org/sites/default/files/medias/fichiers/2025/08/EDS-3-ISCED-Final-WEB.pdf), is defined as an intermediate phase of education spanning ages 11 to 18. The dataset also includes global versions of these measures.

```{r include = FALSE}
# Loading packages
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(countrycode)
library(janitor)
library(scales)
library(gt)
library(gtExtras)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

# Preparing the data

# Loading the population dataset
populations <- countrypops %>%
  filter(year == 2023) %>%
  select(country_code_3, population)

# Loading the HDR dataset
data <- read_excel("hdr-data.xlsx") %>%
  select(-c(yearStr, value, indexCode, index, dimension, note)) %>%
  mutate((across(c(year, actualValue), as.numeric)),
         continent = countrycode(countryIsoCode,
                                 origin = "iso3c",
                                 destination = "continent"),
         # NRO is for Naoero, a country in Oceania
         # ZZK.WORLD means the global value
         continent = ifelse(countryIsoCode == "NRO", "Oceania", continent)) %>%
  # Joining it with populations
  left_join(populations, by = c("countryIsoCode" = "country_code_3"))

# Checking for missing values
colSums(is.na(data))
# 218 NAs in "continent", but these are just world values instead
unique(data[is.na(data$continent), ]$countryIsoCode) # ZZK.WORLD
# 313 NAs in "population", but there are just for the world and Naoero, which
# aren't in the population dataset
unique(data[is.na(data$population), ]$countryIsoCode) # ZZK.WORLD, Naoero

# Checking for duplicate rows
anyDuplicated(data) # 0

# Checking for duplicate (year, country, continent, indicator) combinations because there should
# only be one indicator per country per year
get_dupes(data, year, country, continent, indicator) # no duplicate combinations found
```

### Viewing the global level of education over time

Just as a preliminary look, in this initial plot of the average amount of education worldwide in years, it's clear that the world is gradually becoming more educated as a whole:

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years"),
                     limits = c(NA, 9)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults* Have Worldwide (1990-2023)",
       caption = "*Adults 25+") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14))

# Getting the annual change in MYS per year

mys_1990 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 1990) %>%
  pull(actualValue)

mys_2023 <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", is.na(continent), year == 2023) %>%
  pull(actualValue)
```

The world's education level in general has been steadily growing for the past 3 decades from \~`r round(mys_1990, 1)` years in 1990 to \~`r round(mys_2023, 1)` years in 2023 (a change of \~`r round(mys_2023 - mys_1990, 1)` years!), which is nice to see. In fact, it has gotten better every year, at a rate of \~`r round((mys_2023 - mys_1990) / (2023 - 1990), 1)` years each year.

However, if we look into how the level of education varies by gender and geographically, some disparities do emerge...

### Examining differences by gender

In this plot, when the metric is split by gender, a gap emerges:

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>%
  mutate(indicatorCode = recode(indicatorCode,
                                "mys_f" = "Females",
                                "mys_m" = "Males")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, colour = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Males" = "royalblue2",
                                "Females" = "violetred1")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults Have Worldwide (1990-2023)",
       colour = "") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9))
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Getting the yearly gaps
gen_gaps_avg <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("mys_f", "mys_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gap = mys_m - mys_f)
```

The average amount of education for females has never been more than for males. Although they've been increasing at very similar speeds --- the lines are nearly parallel --- there has consistently been a gap of around a year between them. Nonetheless, over the past few years, beginning in 2020, that gap has been shrinking a little; in 2020, the magnitude of the gap dropped to a new low of ~`r round(filter(gen_gaps_avg, year == 2020)$gap, 1)` years, to ~`r round(filter(gen_gaps_avg, year == 2021)$gap, 1)` years in 2021, ~`r round(filter(gen_gaps_avg, year == 2022)$gap, 1)` years in 2022, and ~`r round(filter(gen_gaps_avg, year == 2023)$gap, 1)` years in 2023.

Another way to look at the gender gap is through the percentage of adults in each gender who have at least some level of secondary education:

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the percentage of people who have secondary education by gender over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"),
         is.na(continent)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = actualValue, fill = indicatorCode)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("se_m" = "royalblue2", "se_f" = "violetred1"),
                    labels = c("se_m" = "Males", "se_f" = "Females")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Percentage of Adults With Secondary Education Worldwide (1990-2023)") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14),
        legend.position = c(0.1, 0.9)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE))
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Getting the yearly gaps
gen_gaps_pct <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode %in% c("se_f", "se_m"), is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year, indicatorCode) %>%
  summarize(actualValue = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = indicatorCode, values_from = actualValue, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(gap = se_m - se_f)
```

Again, the percentage of females with education worldwide has never exceeded the percentage of males, with a consistent difference of `r round(mean(gen_gaps_pct$gap), 1)` raw percentage points, but this has shrunk to \~`r round(filter(gen_gaps_pct, year == 2023)$gap, 1)` raw percentage points in 2023.

I also visualized these percentages across countries for both males and females for 2023, the most recent year in the data. I considered making an animated map showing each year; however, I decided to only plot 2023 because the animated map might be too busy to interpret.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
# Loading world map data
world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>%
  # Joining it with the main data
  left_join(data, by = c("iso_a3" = "countryIsoCode"), suffix = c("_ne", "_data")) %>%
  # Filtering for 2023 only and removing Antarctica
  filter(year == 2023, iso_a3 != "ATA")

# Mapping male percentages
world %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "se_m") %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = actualValue),
          show.legend = "polygon",
          color = "white",
          size = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "Blues",
                       n.breaks = 6,
                       labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
                       name = "% of Males") +
  labs(title = "2023 Percentages of Males With Secondary Education",
       subtitle = "TODO: A Subtitle") +
  theme_void()

# Mapping female percentages
world %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "se_f") %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = actualValue),
          show.legend = "polygon",
          color = "white",
          size = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_fermenter(palette = "RdPu",
                       n.breaks = 6,
                       labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"),
                       name = "% of Females") +
  labs(title = "2023 Percentages of Females With Secondary Education",
       subtitle = "TODO: A Subtitle") +
  theme_void()
```

Next, I turn to the average amount of education for adults, just as a more general, holistic measure that's not split by gender so that explicit geographic differences can be contrasted.

### Examining differences by location

Below is a graph of each continent's average amount of education of adults over 25.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Graphing the global education mean by continent over time
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys",
         !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(continent, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mys = mean(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_mys, colour = continent)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Average Amount of Education That Adults Have (1990-2023)",
       colour = "Continent") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = ~ paste(.x, "Years")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(t = 0, r = 15, b = 0, l = 0)),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(type = "qual", palette = 6)
```

Here are the countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, in terms of the average amount of education of its population over 25 years. There are `r n_distinct(data$countryIsoCode)` countries in total.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Making a table of the least educated countries (1990-2023)
bottom_countries <- data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(actualValue, ties.method = "min")) %>%
  filter(rank <= 10) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  count(continent, country, name = "times_in_bottom_10")

# Making a table of the countries with consistently low education rates
bottom_countries %>%
  arrange(desc(times_in_bottom_10)) %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             times_in_bottom_10 = "# of Times in Bottom 10") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With Consistently Low Education Rates (1990-2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

There are 17 countries that have been in the bottom 10 at least once, of which 4 countries (Afghanistan, Guinea, Mali, and Niger) have been there in every year from 1990 to 2023.

To illustrate the widest global gaps, here are the differences between the highest and lowest-ranked countries over the years.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Putting the yearly gaps in a table
data %>%
  filter(indicatorCode == "mys", !is.na(continent)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(Highest = country[which.max(actualValue)],
            Lowest = country[which.min(actualValue)],
            Gap = round(max(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE) - min(actualValue, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(year = "Year") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Gaps in Education Across Countries Over Time") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95")
```

The gap has remained the same, mostly because the rate of growth has been similar around the world.

Here are the top 5 countries in 2023, again in terms of the average time spent in education of the portion of its population who are over 25.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Making a table of the most educated countries in 2023
data %>%
  filter(year == 2023, indicatorCode == "mys") %>%
  arrange(desc(actualValue)) %>%
  mutate(difference_from_world = actualValue - mys_2023) %>%
  select(continent, country, actualValue, population, difference_from_world) %>%
  head(n = 5) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = population,
             decimals = 0) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             actualValue = "Mean Years of Education",
             population = "Population*",
             difference_from_world = "Distance From World Average") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With the Highest Education Rates (2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95") %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*The population value is the country's entire measured population, not necessarily how many people were used to calculate the mean.")
```

And here are the bottom 20. I'm including more observations in this table because the lower end of the range is more revealing than the upper end.

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Making a table of the least educated countries in 2023
data %>%

  arrange(actualValue) %>%
  mutate(difference_from_world = actualValue - mys_2023) %>%
  select(continent, country, actualValue, population, difference_from_world) %>%
  head(n = 20) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(decimals = 1) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = population,
             decimals = 0) %>%
  cols_align("center") %>%
  cols_label(continent = "Continent",
             country = "Country",
             actualValue = "Mean Years of Education",
             population = "Population*",
             difference_from_world = "Distance From World Average") %>%
  tab_header(title = "Countries With the Lowest Education Rates (2023)") %>%
  tab_style(style = cell_text(size = px(18)),
            locations = cells_title(groups = "title")) %>%
  tab_options(table.border.top.color = "white",
              column_labels.background.color = "grey95") %>%
  tab_source_note(source_note = "*The population value is the country's entire measured population, not necessarily how many people were used to calculate the mean.")
```
